questions.q: What mathematical operation does a perceptron perform on its inputs before applying the activation function?
What does 'linearly separable' mean for a classification problem?
options: A single straight line (or hyperplane) can perfectly separate the classes
The data can be sorted in order
The features have a linear relationship with the label
The data has only two dimensions

questions.q: Why does a single perceptron fail to learn the XOR function?
options: The step function prevents gradient flow
The learning rate is too low
XOR is not linearly separable -- no single line can separate the classes

questions.q: In the perceptron learning rule, what happens when the prediction matches the target?
options: Nothing changes -- error is zero so the update is zero

questions.q: How is XOR solved using multiple perceptrons?
options: By adding more inputs to a single perceptron
By using a larger learning rate on a single perceptron
By combining OR, NAND, and AND perceptrons in two layers

questions.q: What is the purpose of a hidden layer in a multi-layer network?
options: To transform inputs into new feature representations that enable nonlinear decision boundaries
To reduce the number of parameters

questions.q: What does the forward pass do in a neural network?
options: Pushes input through each layer to produce an output

questions.q: For a layer with 3 neurons receiving input from 2 neurons, what is the shape of the weight matrix?
What does the Universal Approximation Theorem guarantee?
options: Neural networks can solve any computational problem
A single hidden layer with enough neurons can approximate any continuous function
Deeper networks always outperform shallow ones
Any network can be trained in polynomial time

questions.q: Why does the sigmoid activation function make learning possible, unlike the step function used in perceptrons?
options: Sigmoid is smooth and differentiable everywhere, so gradients exist for backpropagation

questions.q: What is the chain rule in the context of neural networks?
options: A rule for chaining layers together
If y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f'(g(x)) * g'(x) -- multiply derivatives along the path

questions.q: Why is backpropagation more efficient than computing each gradient independently?
options: It computes all gradients in a single backward pass instead of one forward pass per parameter
It only works on small networks
It avoids using the chain rule

questions.q: In the backward pass, why do we use '+=' instead of '=' when accumulating gradients?
options: A value might be used in multiple operations, so its gradient is the sum of gradients from all paths
It makes the code run faster

questions.q: What causes the vanishing gradient problem in deep sigmoid networks?
options: The loss function is poorly chosen
The network has too many parameters
The learning rate is too small
Sigmoid's derivative has a maximum of 0.25, so gradients shrink exponentially through layers

questions.q: Why does topological sort matter in the backward pass?
options: It speeds up the forward pass
It ensures each node's gradient is fully accumulated before propagating to its children

questions.q: Why can't you build a useful deep network using only linear layers (no activation functions)?
options: Stacking linear layers collapses to a single linear transformation, giving no benefit from depth
Linear layers can't handle batched data

questions.q: What is the output range of the ReLU activation function?
What is the 'dead neuron' problem in ReLU networks?
options: Neurons whose input is permanently negative, producing zero output and zero gradient forever

questions.q: Which activation function is the default for hidden layers in modern transformers like GPT and BERT?
Why is softmax used only in the output layer and never in hidden layers?
options: It only works with two classes
It converts a vector into a probability distribution (values sum to 1), which is needed for classification output but not for intermediate representations
It's too slow for hidden layers

questions.q: What does the loss function represent in neural network training?
options: A differentiable measure of how wrong the model's predictions are, which the optimizer minimizes
The size of the training dataset

questions.q: Why is cross-entropy preferred over MSE for classification tasks?
options: Cross-entropy punishes confident wrong predictions exponentially via -log(p), while MSE gives weak gradients near 0 and 1

questions.q: What happens if you use MSE loss for binary classification?
options: The model can minimize loss by predicting 0.5 for everything, achieving MSE=0.25 without learning

questions.q: What does label smoothing do and why is it useful?
options: It smooths the learning rate schedule
It replaces hard 0/1 targets with soft values like 0.1/0.9, preventing overconfident predictions and improving generalization
It removes noisy labels from the dataset
It applies a moving average to the loss

questions.q: In contrastive loss (InfoNCE), what role does the temperature parameter play?
options: It controls how sharp the similarity distribution is -- lower temperature means harder separation between positives and negatives
It sets the number of negative samples

questions.q: What problem does momentum solve in gradient descent?
options: It eliminates the need for a learning rate
It dampens oscillation by accumulating past gradients, accelerating movement in consistent directions

questions.q: What is the key difference between Adam and AdamW?
options: AdamW uses a higher learning rate
AdamW applies weight decay directly to weights instead of through the gradient, giving proper regularization

questions.q: Why does Adam use bias correction in early training steps?
options: The moment estimates are initialized to zero, so early values are biased toward zero; correction compensates for this cold start

questions.q: What are the standard default hyperparameters for Adam?
Which optimizer is the modern default for training transformers and LLMs?
What is overfitting in neural networks?
options: The model is too small to learn the data
The model memorizes training data instead of learning generalizable patterns, showing a large gap between train and test accuracy

questions.q: How does dropout regularize a neural network?
options: It removes the worst-performing neurons permanently
It randomly zeroes neurons during training, forcing the network to learn redundant representations
It removes outliers from the training data

questions.q: Why do transformers use LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm?
options: LayerNorm normalizes across features per sample (batch-independent), which works with variable sequence lengths and small batch sizes

questions.q: What is the key difference between RMSNorm and LayerNorm?
options: RMSNorm skips the mean subtraction, only dividing by the root mean square, giving ~10% speedup with equal accuracy

questions.q: Why is it critical to call model.eval() before running inference in PyTorch?
options: It disables dropout and switches BatchNorm to use running statistics instead of batch statistics, giving deterministic outputs

questions.q: What happens if you initialize all weights in a neural network to zero?
options: Zero init is the recommended default
The network trains normally but slowly
All neurons compute identical outputs and receive identical gradients, so the network has only 1 effective neuron per layer

questions.q: Why does the scale of random weight initialization matter?
options: Scale only matters for the output layer
If variance is too high, activations explode; if too low, activations vanish -- both prevent training
It doesn't matter as long as weights are nonzero

questions.q: What is the formula for Kaiming/He initialization variance?
When should you use Xavier/Glorot initialization instead of Kaiming/He?
options: When using sigmoid or tanh activations, which don't zero half the outputs like ReLU

questions.q: Why does GPT-2 scale residual layer weights by 1/sqrt(2N)?
options: Each residual addition increases variance, so scaling prevents the accumulated signal from growing unbounded through N layers
To reduce the number of parameters

questions.q: Why is a constant learning rate usually suboptimal for training neural networks?
options: It's either too high for late training (causes oscillation) or too low for early training (wastes compute)

questions.q: What is the purpose of learning rate warmup?
options: To let adaptive optimizer statistics (momentum, variance) stabilize before taking large steps
To increase the batch size gradually

questions.q: What learning rate schedule do Llama 3, GPT-3, and most modern LLMs use?
options: Linear warmup followed by cosine decay

questions.q: What makes the 1cycle policy different from other schedules?
options: It uses a constant learning rate
It ramps the learning rate UP in the first half of training, then back down -- the high LR phase acts as regularization

questions.q: If training loss suddenly spikes and diverges, what is the most likely learning rate issue?
options: Learning rate is too high, causing the optimizer to overshoot the minimum
The warmup period is too long

questions.q: What three responsibilities does the Module abstraction have in a deep learning framework?
options: Load data, preprocess data, augment data
forward() for computation, backward() for gradients, parameters() for trainable weights

questions.q: Why does Sequential process modules in reverse order during the backward pass?
options: Gradients flow from the loss backward through the network, so the last layer computes gradients first

questions.q: Why is optimizer.zero_grad() a separate call instead of being done automatically?
options: It allows gradient accumulation across multiple batches before taking a single optimizer step

questions.q: What is the correct order of operations in a training loop?
What is the role of the DataLoader in the framework?
options: It splits data into batches and optionally shuffles between epochs for mini-batch gradient descent

questions.q: What is autograd in PyTorch?
options: An automatic differentiation engine that records operations and computes gradients without manual backward implementations

questions.q: What does torch.no_grad() do and when should you use it?
options: It disables gradient tracking for inference, saving memory and computation when you don't need to train

questions.q: What does nn.Linear(784, 256) create in PyTorch?
options: A fully connected layer with a (256, 784) weight matrix and a (256,) bias vector

questions.q: Which PyTorch method computes gradients for all parameters in the computational graph?
Why is PyTorch's training loop significantly faster than the pure-Python mini framework?
options: PyTorch runs operations as optimized C++/CUDA kernels on GPU, while pure Python loops are interpreted one operation at a time

questions.q: What is the fundamental design difference between PyTorch and JAX?
options: PyTorch mutates tensors eagerly while JAX compiles pure functions without side effects

questions.q: What does jax.jit do?
options: It compiles a Python function into optimized XLA code that runs much faster than interpreted Python

questions.q: What does jax.vmap do?
options: Vectorizes a function to run over a batch dimension without writing explicit loops

questions.q: How does JAX handle model state (weights) differently than PyTorch?
options: JAX requires explicit state passing -- weights are function arguments, not mutable object attributes
JAX and PyTorch handle state identically
JAX stores weights on CPU only

questions.q: When would you choose JAX over PyTorch?
options: When you need the largest ecosystem of pretrained models
For quick prototyping of small models
When training at massive scale on TPU pods, where compilation and functional transforms provide significant speedups

questions.q: Why is neural network debugging harder than traditional software debugging?
options: There are no debugging tools for neural networks
Networks can produce wrong outputs without any error messages or crashes -- the code runs but the results are silently incorrect
Neural networks use different programming languages

questions.q: What is the 'overfit one batch' debugging technique?
options: Training on the full dataset until it overfits
Using a very large batch size
Training on a single small batch until the loss reaches near-zero, verifying the model can memorize at least a few examples

questions.q: Your loss is NaN after a few training steps. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model has too few parameters
Exploding gradients or numerical overflow, often from a learning rate that's too high or missing gradient clipping

questions.q: Your training loss decreases but validation loss stays flat from the start. What does this indicate?
options: The model is learning training data patterns but they don't generalize -- likely a data pipeline issue (train/val data mismatch) or severe overfitting
The learning rate is too low

questions.q: What should you check first when your loss curve is completely flat (loss doesn't decrease at all)?
options: Verify gradients are nonzero, the learning rate is high enough, and the loss function actually depends on the model's predictions
